title: Twelve baskets left (John 6:1–15)
hook: gather the fragments so nothing is lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus called his witnesses, and the last was a book. Your line was the scriptures point to him. Which verse did you read, and who did it show you? Day six hundred eight.

Five thousand people on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee, and it's getting late. John notes that Passover is near, the spring feast that remembers bread in a hurry and manna in the desert. Jesus looks at the crowd and asks Philip a question, as a test: where shall we buy bread for all these? Philip does the math and gives up: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." A penny there is a day's wage. Two hundred days of work wouldn't buy everyone a bite. Then Andrew notices a boy.

Andrew says: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Only John mentions the boy, and only John says the loaves were barley, the cheap bread, the bread of poor families. A kid's lunch, offered to a crowd. Jesus has everyone sit down on the grass. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Everyone eats until they're full. The Gospels don't describe how it happened. They only describe what people saw: enough. Then comes the part this day is named for. Jesus says to the disciples: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They go around the hillside collecting broken pieces, and they fill twelve baskets. Think about that instruction. A miracle has just happened, and the next thing Jesus cares about is the crumbs. Nothing wasted. Nothing thrown away. Twelve baskets, one for each disciple doing the gathering, maybe, or a number many readers connect with the twelve tribes of Israel. The feeding of the crowd is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell. Christians have often heard it as a picture of the Lord's Supper too: he took bread, gave thanks, and gave it. And the scene ends strangely. The crowd is so excited they want to seize Jesus and make him king by force. And he slips away alone, up the mountain. He came to feed them, not to be crowned by them.

Here's the practice: use up leftovers. Settle, and breathe. Picture your kitchen. What's sitting in the fridge or the cupboard that might get thrown out? Half a loaf, a few vegetables, last night's rice. Make a plan to use one thing today. Then widen it. What else in your life is a fragment you've stopped noticing? A half-finished letter. An hour you usually waste. A small skill nobody asks for. If you pray, you can give thanks for what's already there, the way Jesus gave thanks over a boy's lunch. If you don't, simply notice how much is there. The bell holds the time.
Twelve baskets left. After five thousand ate, the disciples gathered the fragments, so that nothing would be lost.
Your line: let nothing be lost. Today, cook or eat one leftover instead of throwing it out, and notice one other thing worth saving. Day six hundred eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians give thanks before meals, as Jesus does here, and churches often run food banks and community meals, gathering surplus food so nothing is wasted.

fork.setup: five thousand people have just eaten their fill. you're a disciple. what does Jesus ask you to do next?
options: ask the boy for more food.
fork.reveal: "gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." they fill twelve baskets.

original.note: Greek: broken pieces, fragments. The word for what was left over.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a miracle of lots of food.
what it means: a boy's small lunch becomes enough, and Jesus makes sure even the crumbs aren't wasted.
what a scholar hears: John sets the scene near Passover, and many readers hear echoes of manna in the desert and of the Lord's Supper in "took, gave thanks, gave."

notes: KJV 'penny' = denarius, a day's wage (cf. Matthew 20:2). Confirm.
Barley bread as the cheaper bread of the poor: common commentary claim. Confirm.
'The only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell': common claim; confirm.
Twelve baskets linked to twelve disciples or twelve tribes: given as readings, not fact.
The script says the Gospels don't describe how the multiplication happened; confirm wording is acceptable across churches.
